catalog_quote: Stress: Each Hiri Motu word contains only one stressed syllable, the placement of which is not predictable. i) words consisting of two syllables of which the second begins with a consonant have their stress (marked ´ in examples) mostly on the first syllable, e.g.: gíni 'to stand', áne 'song'. Exceptions: idáu 'different', dogái 'widower', metáu 'heavy', niú 'coconut', heáu 'to run', heái 'to fight'. ii) words of more than two syllables never have their stress on the final syllable, e.g.: bogakúnu 'full (with food)', dábarere 'dawn'. iii) words of more than two syllables are variously stressed depending on morphemic structure, e.g.: kubórukubóru 'round', dogoatáo 'to hold', magánibada 'ridge pole', dúrua 'to help', taunimánima 'people', hadikáia 'to spoil'. iv) in a few instances the position of the stress in a word undergoes regular changes when a suffix is added, e.g.: námo 'good', na…
sweep_summary: The search of works with stress or accent in the title for Hiri Motu (hiri1237, catalog classification lexical, deciding source Dutton & Brown 1977) contains a single item, Himmelmann & Ladd 2008 'Prosodic Description: An Introduction for Fieldworkers' (LD&C 2(2)). It was already held by the project and was re-read in full: it is a general prosodic-fieldwork tutorial with no Hiri Motu content at all (zero hits for Motu/Hiri/Papua New Guinea in the text). The Glottolog 5.3 record (saved) states verbatim that the language code was a 'computerized assignment from \"fieldworkers\"' and the listed by Glottolog as a grammar a 'computerized assignment from \"description\"' — i.e. a Glottolog artefact, so it should be dropped from or flagged in the hiri1237 bibliography. Relevance not relevant, silent on the catalog, priority none. No new works with stress in the title bears on the classification. As a by-product, the on-disk Wurm & Harris 1963 Police Motu (PL-B1) was read for its stress statements (p. 1 and pp. 54-55): stress is marked with an acute because it is not fully predictable and varies regionally, final vowels are rarely stressed, and the suffixes -na/-dia put main stress on the preceding syllable — this confirms and mildly refines the catalog's 'lexical' coding but does not supersede Dutton & Brown 1977. Dutton & Voorhoeve 1974 (PL-D24, held by the project) has no general stress statement. the Glottolog and ScholarSpace pages were downloaded directly.

new_statements.quote: p.1: "An attempt has been made to indicate the incidence of strongest stress by the use of the acute (´). We are aware that this is not really satisfactory and that practice varies considerably from place to place. In the pronunciation presented here, final vowels are only rarely stressed. We have indicated stress on disyllabic words only when it is on the final syllable, and also when perhaps some doubt may arise in the minds of the readers as to its placement." p.54-55: "both -na and -dia cause the main stress to fall on the syllable preceding them" ... "The main stress falls on the syllable preceding -na or -dia." (scanned letter-spacing removed; wording as printed)

new_statements.reading: First-hand statement for Police Motu (= Hiri Motu) by Wurm & Harris: stress placement has to be marked with an acute because it is not fully predictable and varies regionally; final syllables are rarely stressed, so unmarked disyllables are to be read as initially stressed; the suffixes -na / -dia attract main stress to the syllable immediately before them (i.e. penult of the suffixed form). This is consistent with, and slightly earlier than, the catalog's Dutton & Brown 1977 statement ('only one stressed syllable, the placement of which is not predictable'; disyllables mostly initial with listed exceptions). It CONFIRMS the catalog's 'lexical' coding and REFINES it with the -na/-dia pre-suffix stress rule; it does not supersede Dutton & Brown 1977, which is fuller and more explicit about unpredictability. Note: Dutton & Voorhoeve 1974 (PL-D24, also held by the project) has no general stress statement, only incidental acute marks (e.g. iéna, p. 19).

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated pages/section in the PL-C40 file we hold. The deciding work is the standard linguistic sketch of Hiri Motu by Dutton & Brown (1977); The one independent earlier description, Wurm & Harris 1963 (downloaded), marks stress lexically, says finals are rarely stressed and that -na/-dia pull stress to the preceding syllable — matching our lexical coding and its stated sub-regularities. Only Dutton 1997 (paywalled Benjamins chapter) remains unseen and is unlikely to alter the classification.
